stem.en: At chemical equilibrium:

options.en: the rates of the forward and backward reactions are equal
the forward and backward reactions stop
the concentrations of reactants and products are always equal

explanation.en: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal).

stem.en: When a bottle of soda water is opened, it fizzes. This is best explained by:

explanation.en: The CO₂ dissolved under high pressure; on opening, its pressure falls and, by Henry's law, its solubility falls, so gas escapes.

stem.en: Ice and water are in equilibrium at 1 atm. The temperature of this system is:

explanation.en: The normal melting point of ice is 273 K (0 °C); at this temperature ice and water coexist at 1 atm.

stem.en: Using a mixture of H₂ and D₂ in the Haber process shows that ammonia containing deuterium forms even after equilibrium. This proves that equilibrium is:

options.en: reached only from the reactant side

explanation.en: Deuterium keeps getting into ammonia, so the forward and backward reactions are still going on at equilibrium: it is dynamic.

solution.en: Deuterium keeps getting into ammonia, so the forward and backward reactions are still going on at equilibrium: it is dynamic.

stem.en: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of chemical equilibrium?

options.en: A catalyst changes the equilibrium composition
It is possible only in a closed system
It can be reached from either direction

explanation.en: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally; it shortens the time to reach equilibrium but does not change the composition.

stem.en: For which reaction is Kp = Kc?

explanation.en: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so Kp = Kc(RT)⁰ = Kc.

stem.en: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), Kp equals:

explanation.en: Pure solids are left out of the expression, so Kp = p(CO₂).

stem.en: The unit of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is:

explanation.en: Kc = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) has unit (mol L⁻¹)^(2−4) = (mol L⁻¹)⁻² = L² mol⁻².

stem.en: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) the equilibrium constant is K. The equilibrium constant for SO₃(g) ⇌ SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) is:

explanation.en: Reversing gives 1/K; halving the equation takes the square root: (1/K)^½ = 1/√K.

solution.en: Reversing gives 1/K; halving the equation takes the square root: (1/K)^½ = 1/√K.

stem.en: 1.0 mol each of A and B are placed in a 1 L flask. For A + B ⇌ C + D, Kc = 4. The equilibrium concentration of C is:
If the reaction quotient Q is less than K, the reaction:

explanation.en: Q < K means products are too few; the reaction moves forward until Q = K.

stem.en: A catalyst added to a system at equilibrium:

options.en: helps the system reach equilibrium faster without changing K

explanation.en: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both forward and backward reactions equally; K is unchanged.

stem.en: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹, the yield of ammonia is increased by:

options.en: adding an inert gas at constant volume

explanation.en: Four gas moles go to two, so high pressure helps; the reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature increases K.

stem.en: For an equilibrium with K > 1 at 298 K, ΔG° is:

explanation.en: ΔG° = −RT ln K; ln K > 0 when K > 1, so ΔG° < 0.

solution.en: ΔG° = −RT ln K; ln K > 0 when K > 1, so ΔG° < 0.

stem.en: Argon is added to the equilibrium PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at constant volume. The equilibrium:

options.en: shifts forward only if the temperature is high

explanation.en: At constant volume the partial pressures (concentrations) of the reacting gases do not change, so Q stays equal to K: no shift.

stem.en: Which of the following is a Lewis acid?

explanation.en: BF₃ has an incomplete octet on boron and accepts an electron pair.

stem.en: The conjugate base of HCO₃⁻ is:

explanation.en: Removing one H⁺ from HCO₃⁻ gives CO₃²⁻.

stem.en: The pH of 0.001 M HCl is:

explanation.en: HCl is a strong acid: [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M, so pH = 3.

stem.en: The pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl at 298 K is about:

explanation.en: Water's own H⁺ cannot be neglected: x² − 10⁻⁸x − 10⁻¹⁴ = 0 gives [H⁺] ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M, pH ≈ 6.98 (an acid can never have pH 8).

solution.en: Water's own H⁺ cannot be neglected: x² − 10⁻⁸x − 10⁻¹⁴ = 0 gives [H⁺] ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M, pH ≈ 6.98 (an acid can never have pH 8).

stem.en: When pure water is heated from 25 °C to 60 °C:

options.en: Kw decreases and water becomes basic
Kw increases, pH falls below 7 but water stays neutral

explanation.en: Ionisation of water is endothermic, so Kw rises with temperature. [H⁺] = [OH⁻] still, so water stays neutral though its pH is below 7.

stem.en: The aqueous solution of which salt is acidic?

explanation.en: NH₄Cl is a salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a weak base (NH₃); NH₄⁺ hydrolyses to give H⁺.

stem.en: The pH of 0.1 M solution of a weak monobasic acid with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ is:
Adding sodium acetate to a solution of acetic acid:

options.en: increases the ionisation of acetic acid
suppresses the ionisation of acetic acid and raises the pH

explanation.en: The common ion CH₃COO⁻ pushes CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ back, lowering [H⁺], so pH rises.

stem.en: Ka of HCN is 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 298 K. Kb of CN⁻ is:
A buffer is made of an acid of pKa 4.74 and its sodium salt, with [salt]/[acid] = 10. Its pH is:
A precipitate forms when:

explanation.en: When the ionic product exceeds Ksp the solution is supersaturated and the excess salt precipitates.

stem.en: For a sparingly soluble salt of type AB₂ with solubility s, Ksp is:

explanation.en: AB₂ ⇌ A²⁺ + 2B⁻: Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³.

stem.en: The solubility of AgCl is lowest in:

explanation.en: Cl⁻ is a common ion; the highest [Cl⁻] (0.1 M NaCl) suppresses solubility the most.

stem.en: The solubility product of Ca₃(PO₄)₂ in terms of its molar solubility s is:

explanation.en: [Ca²⁺] = 3s, [PO₄³⁻] = 2s: Ksp = (3s)³(2s)² = 27 × 4 s⁵ = 108s⁵.

stem.en: The molar solubility of Mg(OH)₂ is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Its Ksp is:

Assertion (A): Increasing the pressure on the equilibrium H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) shifts it to the right.
Reason (R): The number of moles of gas is the same on both sides of this equation.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: A is false: since Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, a change of pressure does not shift this equilibrium. R is true and is the reason pressure has no effect.

passage.en: An ammonia plant runs the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. The plant manager wants a larger equilibrium yield of ammonia from the same feed of nitrogen and hydrogen. Four engineers each suggest one change to the reactor conditions.

stem.en: Which suggested change would increase the equilibrium yield of ammonia?

options.en: Raise the temperature of the reactor

explanation.en: 4 mol of gas → 2 mol of gas, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium right (Le Chatelier). The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating shifts it left. A catalyst only helps reach equilibrium faster; it does not change the yield.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): An aqueous solution of sodium acetate is basic.
Reason (R): The acetate ion reacts with water to form acetic acid and hydroxide ions.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Both true; R explains A. CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻: the salt of a weak acid and a strong base undergoes anionic hydrolysis, raising [OH⁻] so pH > 7.

passage.en: A biology lab needs a buffer for an enzyme experiment. A student dissolves 0.10 mol of acetic acid and 0.20 mol of sodium acetate in water and makes the solution up to 1.0 L. The pKa of acetic acid is 4.76 (log 2 = 0.30).

stem.en: What is the pH of the buffer the student has prepared?
For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹, which of the following increase the equilibrium yield of NH₃? One or more options may be correct.

explanation.en: High pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (2 < 4). The forward reaction is exothermic, so lower T favours it. A catalyst only speeds up the approach to equilibrium. Removing product shifts it forward.

stem.en: Which of the following mixtures act as buffer solutions? One or more options may be correct.

explanation.en: A buffer is a weak acid (or base) with its conjugate. Acetic acid/acetate, ammonia/ammonium and H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻ are such pairs. HCl is a strong acid, so HCl + NaCl is not a buffer.

stem.en: Calculate the pH of 0.01 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵). Give your answer to two decimal places.
The solubility product of Ag₂CrO₄ is 1.1 × 10⁻¹². What is its solubility in water in units of 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹? Give your answer to two decimal places.

explanation.en: Ag₂CrO₄ ⇌ 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻, so Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³. s³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹²/4 = 2.75 × 10⁻¹³, s = 6.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹.

stem.en: For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the relation between Kp and Kc is:

explanation.en: Δn = moles of gaseous products − reactants = 2 − 4 = −2, so Kp = Kc(RT)⁻².

solution.en: Δn = moles of gaseous products − reactants = 2 − 4 = −2, so Kp = Kc(RT)⁻².

stem.en: The pH of a 0.005 M solution of Ba(OH)₂ (fully ionised) at 298 K is:

explanation.en: Each Ba(OH)₂ gives 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.01 M, pOH = 2 and pH = 14 − 2 = 12.

solution.en: Each Ba(OH)₂ gives 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.01 M, pOH = 2 and pH = 14 − 2 = 12.

stem.en: The equilibrium constant for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is K. The equilibrium constant for SO₃(g) ⇌ SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) at the same temperature is:

explanation.en: Reversing the equation gives 1/K; halving the coefficients takes the square root: (1/K)^½ = 1/√K.

stem.en: The pH of a 0.005 M H₂SO₄ solution (assume complete dissociation) is:

explanation.en: Each H₂SO₄ gives 2 H⁺: $[\text{H}^+] = 2 \times 0.005 = 0.01$ M, so pH $= -\log 10^{-2} = 2$. (2.3 forgets the factor of 2.)

stem.en: For $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$, the relation between $K_p$ and $K_c$ is:

explanation.en: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$ and $\Delta n_g = 2 - 4 = -2$, so $K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2}$.

stem.en: Ammonia synthesis, $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$, is exothermic. Raising the temperature at equilibrium will:

explanation.en: By Le Chatelier's principle, heating favours the endothermic (backward) direction. For an exothermic reaction $K$ decreases as temperature rises, lowering the NH₃ yield.

options.en: shift the equilibrium backward and decrease $K$
shift the equilibrium forward and increase $K$
not change the position of equilibrium

stem.en: If $s$ is the molar solubility of Ag₂CrO₄, its solubility product is:

explanation.en: $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}^+ + \text{CrO}_4^{2-}$: $K_{sp} = (2s)^2(s) = 4s^3$.

stem.en: A buffer contains 0.02 M acetic acid and 0.2 M sodium acetate. If $\text{p}K_a$ of acetic acid is 4.74, the pH of the buffer is:

explanation.en: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH $= \text{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} = 4.74 + \log 10 = 5.74$.

stem.en: PCl₅ dissociates as $\text{PCl}_5 \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3 + \text{Cl}_2$. At a total equilibrium pressure of 1 atm, it is 50% dissociated. $K_p$ is about:

explanation.en: Start with 1 mol: at equilibrium $1 - \alpha$, $\alpha$, $\alpha$; total $1 + \alpha$. $K_p = \dfrac{(\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}P)^2}{\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}P} = \dfrac{\alpha^2 P}{1 - \alpha^2} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.75} \approx 0.33$ atm.

stem.en: At 25°C an aqueous solution has $[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-4}$ M. What is its pH?

explanation.en: pOH $= 4$. At 25°C, pH + pOH $= 14$, so pH $= 10$.

stem.en: For which of the following equilibria is Kₚ = K_c?

explanation.en: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$. For H$_2$ + I$_2$ ⇌ 2HI, $\Delta n_g = 2 - 2 = 0$, so $K_p = K_c$. The others have $\Delta n_g = -2$, $+1$ and $-1$.

stem.en: The conjugate base of HSO₄⁻ is:

explanation.en: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid loses one proton: HSO$_4^-$ − H$^+$ = SO$_4^{2-}$. H$_2$SO$_4$ is the conjugate acid of HSO$_4^-$.

stem.en: What is the pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution at 298 K?

explanation.en: HCl is a strong acid, fully ionised: $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3}$ M, so pH $= -\log(10^{-3}) = 3$.

stem.en: The ionic product of water Kw increases with temperature. At 60 °C, pure water has:

explanation.en: Ionisation of water is endothermic, so $K_w$ rises with T (about $10^{-13}$ at 60 °C). Then $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_w} > 10^{-7}$, so pH < 7. But $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$ still, so the water is neutral. "pH 7 = neutral" is true only at 25 °C.

stem.en: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium:

explanation.en: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, speeding both equally. It changes neither K nor the equilibrium composition; it only shortens the time needed to reach equilibrium.

options.en: Shifts the equilibrium to the right
Does not change the equilibrium composition but equilibrium is reached faster
Shifts the equilibrium to the left

stem.en: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), increasing the total pressure (by reducing volume) at constant temperature:

explanation.en: Le Chatelier: higher pressure is relieved by moving towards fewer gas molecules. Reactants have 4 mol of gas, products 2, so the equilibrium shifts right and more NH$_3$ forms. K is unchanged because the temperature is constant.

options.en: Shifts the equilibrium to the left
Shifts the equilibrium to the right

stem.en: An aqueous solution of ammonium chloride is:

explanation.en: NH$_4$Cl is a salt of a weak base (NH$_3$) and a strong acid (HCl). NH$_4^+$ hydrolyses: NH$_4^+$ + H$_2$O ⇌ NH$_3$ + H$_3$O$^+$, so the solution is acidic (pH < 7). Cl$^-$ does not hydrolyse.

stem.en: If s is the molar solubility of calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂, its solubility product is:

explanation.en: Ca$_3$(PO$_4$)$_2$ ⇌ 3Ca$^{2+}$ + 2PO$_4^{3-}$: $[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = 3s$, $[\text{PO}_4^{3-}] = 2s$. $K_{sp} = (3s)^3(2s)^2 = 27s^3 \times 4s^2 = 108s^5$. "6 s⁵" multiplies the coefficients instead of raising them to powers.

stem.en: Which of the following can act both as a Brønsted acid and as a Brønsted base?

explanation.en: HCO$_3^-$ can donate a proton (→ CO$_3^{2-}$) or accept one (→ H$_2$CO$_3$), so it is amphiprotic. NH$_4^+$ can only donate; CO$_3^{2-}$ can only accept; Cl$^-$ is an extremely weak base.

stem.en: For the equilibrium CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), the equilibrium constant Kₚ is:

explanation.en: Pure solids have unit activity and are left out of the expression, so $K_p = p_{\text{CO}_2}$. At a given temperature the CO$_2$ pressure over CaCO$_3$ is therefore fixed, however much solid is present.

stem.en: Which of the following mixtures forms a buffer solution?

explanation.en: A buffer is a weak acid with its salt (conjugate base), or a weak base with its salt. Acetic acid + sodium acetate is the classic acidic buffer (pH ≈ pK$_a$ = 4.74 for equal amounts). The other mixtures contain a strong acid or base with its neutral salt and have no reservoir to neutralise added H$^+$/OH$^-$.

stem.en: For 2A(g) ⇌ B(g), K_c = 16 at a certain temperature. The value of K_c for ½B(g) ⇌ A(g) at the same temperature is:

explanation.en: Reversing: B ⇌ 2A, $K = 1/16$. Halving every coefficient takes the square root: $K = (1/16)^{1/2} = 1/4 = 0.25$. 4 forgets to invert; 0.0625 forgets the square root; 8 divides by 2 instead of taking a root.

stem.en: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g) + D(g), K_c = 4.0. At some instant [A] = [B] = [C] = 1.0 M and [D] = 2.0 M. The reaction at this instant:

explanation.en: $Q_c = \dfrac{[\text{C}][\text{D}]}{[\text{A}][\text{B}]} = \dfrac{1 \times 2}{1 \times 1} = 2$. Since $Q < K$ (2 < 4), the system must form more products to reach equilibrium, so the net reaction goes forward.

stem.en: Calculate the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid ($K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}$) at 298 K (to two decimal places).

explanation.en: $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a c} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.10} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-6}} = 1.34\times10^{-3}$ M. pH $= 3 - \log 1.34 = 3 - 0.13 = 2.87$. (α = 1.3%, so the approximation is valid.) pH = 1 would treat acetic acid as a strong acid.

stem.en: A buffer contains 0.20 M CH₃COONa and 0.10 M CH₃COOH (pK_a = 4.74). Its pH is (log 2 = 0.30):

explanation.en: pH $= \text{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} = 4.74 + \log\dfrac{0.20}{0.10} = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04$. 4.44 inverts the ratio; 9.26 is pK$_b$ of acetate.

stem.en: The solubility product of AgCl at 298 K is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. Its molar solubility in pure water is:

explanation.en: AgCl ⇌ Ag$^+$ + Cl$^-$; $K_{sp} = s^2$, so $s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} = 1.34\times10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Writing $s = K_{sp}$, $K_{sp}/2$ or $2K_{sp}$ gives the other values.

stem.en: The molar solubility of AgCl (K_sp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) in 0.010 M NaCl solution is:

explanation.en: Common-ion effect: $[\text{Cl}^-] \approx 0.010$ M, so $s = [\text{Ag}^+] = K_{sp}/[\text{Cl}^-] = 1.8\times10^{-10}/0.010 = 1.8\times10^{-8}$ M — about 750 times less than in pure water ($1.34\times10^{-5}$ M).

stem.en: The pH of a 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl solution at 298 K is approximately:

explanation.en: Let water contribute $x$: $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-8} + x$, $[\text{OH}^-] = x$, and $(10^{-8} + x)x = 10^{-14}$. Solving, $x = 9.5\times10^{-8}$, so $[\text{H}^+] = 1.05\times10^{-7}$ M and pH $= 6.98$. pH = 8 would make an acid solution basic — impossible.

stem.en: 50 mL of 0.10 M HCl is mixed with 50 mL of 0.20 M NaOH at 298 K. What is the pH of the resulting solution (to one decimal place)? (log 5 = 0.70)

explanation.en: H$^+$: $50 \times 0.10 = 5$ mmol; OH$^-$: $50 \times 0.20 = 10$ mmol. Excess OH$^-$ = 5 mmol in 100 mL → 0.050 M. pOH $= -\log 0.05 = 1.30$, pH $= 14 - 1.30 = 12.70$. Forgetting the dilution to 100 mL gives pOH = 1.0, pH = 13.0.

stem.en: The pH of 0.10 M sodium acetate solution at 298 K is (pK_a of acetic acid = 4.74):

explanation.en: Acetate hydrolyses to give OH$^-$. pH $= 7 + \tfrac12\text{p}K_a + \tfrac12\log c = 7 + 2.37 + \tfrac12(-1) = 8.87$. Equivalently, $K_h = K_w/K_a = 5.5\times10^{-10}$, $[\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_h c} = 7.4\times10^{-6}$, pOH = 5.13 — so 5.13 is the pOH, not the pH.

stem.en: PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g). At equilibrium at a total pressure of 1.0 atm, PCl₅ is 50% dissociated. The value of Kₚ is:

explanation.en: Start with 1 mol PCl$_5$: at equilibrium $1 - \alpha$, $\alpha$, $\alpha$; total $1 + \alpha$. $K_p = \dfrac{(\alpha P/(1+\alpha))^2}{(1-\alpha)P/(1+\alpha)} = \dfrac{\alpha^2P}{1 - \alpha^2} = \dfrac{0.25 \times 1}{0.75} = 0.33$ atm. 0.25 atm ignores the $(1 - \alpha^2)$ term; 0.50 atm uses $\alpha^2/(1-\alpha)$ with mole numbers instead of mole fractions.

stem.en: 1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.0 mol of I₂ are heated in a 1.0 L sealed flask. At equilibrium, 0.20 mol of I₂ remains. Calculate K_c for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).

explanation.en: I$_2$ consumed = 0.80 mol, so H$_2$ left = 0.20 mol and HI formed = 1.60 mol. $K_c = \dfrac{(1.60)^2}{(0.20)(0.20)} = \dfrac{2.56}{0.04} = 64$. Taking HI = 0.80 mol (forgetting the coefficient 2) gives 16.

stem.en:
Statement I: Adding argon at constant volume to the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) does not shift the equilibrium.
Statement II: Adding an inert gas at constant total pressure shifts an equilibrium towards the side with more moles of gas.
Choose the correct option.

explanation.en: At constant volume, adding argon raises the total pressure but leaves every reacting gas's concentration (and partial pressure) unchanged, so Q = K and nothing shifts ✓. At constant pressure the volume must increase; this dilutes the reacting gases, which is like lowering pressure, so the system shifts to the side with more gas moles ✓.

options.en: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

stem.en:
Assertion (A): For an exothermic reaction, the equilibrium constant decreases when the temperature is raised.
Reason (R): According to the van 't Hoff equation, log(K₂/K₁) = (ΔH°/2.303R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂), which is negative for ΔH° < 0 and T₂ > T₁.

explanation.en: For T$_2$ > T$_1$, $(1/T_1 - 1/T_2) > 0$; with $\Delta H^\circ < 0$ the right-hand side is negative, so K$_2$ < K$_1$. This is exactly the quantitative form of Le Chatelier's principle for temperature. Both A and R are true and R explains A.

options.en: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

stem.en: A weak monobasic acid solution is diluted to four times its original volume. Its degree of ionisation (α ≪ 1):

explanation.en: $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/c}$. Diluting 4 times makes $c \to c/4$, so $\alpha \to \sqrt{4}\,\alpha = 2\alpha$. Ionisation increases on dilution, even though [H$^+$] $= \sqrt{K_a c}$ falls to half.

stem.en: The correct order of acid strength of the oxoacids of chlorine is:

explanation.en: More O atoms on Cl means a higher oxidation state of Cl and more delocalisation of the negative charge in the conjugate base (ClO$_4^-$ spreads it over four O atoms). The more stable the conjugate base, the stronger the acid: HClO$_4$ > HClO$_3$ > HClO$_2$ > HClO.

stem.en:
Match each Brønsted acid in Column I with its conjugate base in Column II.
Column I: (P) H₂O (Q) HCO₃⁻ (R) NH₃ (S) HSO₄⁻
Column II: (i) NH₂⁻ (ii) OH⁻ (iii) SO₄²⁻ (iv) CO₃²⁻

explanation.en: H$_2$O − H$^+$ = OH$^-$; HCO$_3^-$ − H$^+$ = CO$_3^{2-}$; NH$_3$ − H$^+$ = NH$_2^-$ (amide); HSO$_4^-$ − H$^+$ = SO$_4^{2-}$. Note NH$_3$ acting as an acid (in liquid ammonia), not its usual role as a base.

stem.en: The solubility of CaF₂ in water at 298 K is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Its solubility product is:
Equal volumes of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M AgNO₃ and 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M NaCl are mixed. Given K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰:

explanation.en: After mixing, $[\text{Ag}^+] = [\text{Cl}^-] = 1.0\times10^{-4}$ M. Ionic product $Q = (1.0\times10^{-4})^2 = 1.0\times10^{-8} > K_{sp}$, so AgCl precipitates. The last option reaches the right conclusion with the wrong Q (no allowance for dilution).

options.en: No precipitate forms because Q < K_sp

stem.en: The most suitable indicator for the titration of acetic acid with sodium hydroxide is:

explanation.en: At the equivalence point the solution contains sodium acetate, which hydrolyses to give pH ≈ 8.7. The indicator must change colour in the steep part of the curve around this pH, so phenolphthalein (8.3–10) is chosen. Methyl orange would change colour far too early. The equivalence point is at pH 7 only for strong acid–strong base titrations.

options.en: Any indicator, since the equivalence point is at pH 7

stem.en: K_b for NH₃ is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 298 K. K_a for its conjugate acid NH₄⁺ is:

explanation.en: $K_a = \dfrac{K_w}{K_b} = \dfrac{1.0\times10^{-14}}{1.8\times10^{-5}} = 5.6\times10^{-10}$. Equivalently, p$K_a$ = 14 − 4.74 = 9.26. The weaker a base, the stronger its conjugate acid (and vice versa).

stem.en: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g) + D(g), K_c = 4.0. If 1.0 mol each of A and B are placed in a 1.0 L vessel, how many moles of C are present at equilibrium (to two decimal places)? (in mol)

explanation.en: Let $x$ mol react: $K_c = \dfrac{x^2}{(1 - x)^2} = 4$ ⟹ $\dfrac{x}{1 - x} = 2$ ⟹ $x = 2/3 = 0.67$ mol. Writing $x^2 = 4$ (ignoring the reactants) gives the impossible $x = 2$.

stem.en: The degree of ionisation of 0.010 M aqueous ammonia (K_b = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) at 298 K is about:

explanation.en: $\alpha = \sqrt{K_b/c} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}/0.010} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-3}} = 0.042 = 4.2\%$. (This is still small enough for the approximation to be reasonable.) 0.042% forgets to convert the fraction to a percentage correctly.

stem.en: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Which of the following increase the equilibrium yield of NH₃?

explanation.en: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (products) ✓. The forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering T increases K ✓ (industrially ~700 K is a compromise with rate). Removing product keeps Q < K, pulling the reaction forward ✓. A catalyst only speeds up the attainment of equilibrium ✗.

options.en: Continuously removing NH₃ as it forms

stem.en: Which of the following mixtures act as buffer solutions?

explanation.en: NH$_4$OH/NH$_4$Cl: weak base + its salt ✓. 0.2 mol CH$_3$COOH + 0.1 mol NaOH gives 0.1 mol CH$_3$COOH + 0.1 mol CH$_3$COONa, a buffer with pH = pK$_a$ ✓. HCl + NaCl: strong acid + neutral salt ✗. H$_2$PO$_4^-$/HPO$_4^{2-}$ is a weak acid/conjugate base pair (the blood/cell phosphate buffer, pK$_{a2}$ ≈ 7.2) ✓.

options.en: 0.2 mol CH₃COOH + 0.1 mol NaOH in 1 L
0.1 mol HCl + 0.1 mol NaCl in 1 L

stem.en: Which of the following can act as Lewis acids?

explanation.en: AlCl$_3$: Al has an incomplete octet ✓. SnCl$_4$: Sn can expand its octet using vacant d orbitals (e.g. [SnCl$_6$]$^{2-}$) ✓. Ag$^+$: cations accept electron pairs (e.g. [Ag(NH$_3$)$_2$]$^+$) ✓. NH$_3$ donates its lone pair — a Lewis base ✗.

stem.en: Which of the following statements about the ionisation of water are correct?

explanation.en: 2H$_2$O ⇌ H$_3$O$^+$ + OH$^-$ is endothermic, so $K_w$ increases with T ✓ (≈ $2.5\times10^{-13}$ at 80 °C), making pH ≈ 6.3 while $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$ ✓✓. p$K_w$ = 14 only at 25 °C ✗.

options.en: K_w increases with increase in temperature
Pure water at 80 °C has pH less than 7 but is neutral
In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] at every temperature

stem.en: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). At a total pressure of 1.0 atm and a certain temperature, N₂O₄ is 20% dissociated. Calculate Kₚ (in atm, to two decimal places). (in atm)

explanation.en: From 1 mol N$_2$O$_4$: 0.80 mol N$_2$O$_4$ and 0.40 mol NO$_2$, total 1.20 mol. $p_{\text{NO}_2} = (0.40/1.20)(1) = 1/3$ atm, $p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} = 2/3$ atm. $K_p = \dfrac{(1/3)^2}{2/3} = \dfrac16 = 0.167 \approx 0.17$ atm. Using moles directly ($0.4^2/0.8 = 0.20$) ignores the mole-fraction step.

stem.en: What is the degree of ionisation of acetic acid (K_a = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) in a solution that is 0.10 M in CH₃COOH and 0.010 M in HCl?

explanation.en: $[\text{H}^+] \approx 0.010$ M from HCl (common ion suppresses acetic acid). $K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]} = \dfrac{0.010 \times 0.10\alpha}{0.10}$ ⟹ $\alpha = K_a/0.010 = 1.8\times10^{-3}$. Without HCl α would be $\sqrt{K_a/c} = 1.34\times10^{-2}$ — about 7 times larger.

stem.en: K_sp of Mg(OH)₂ is 1.2 × 10⁻¹¹ at 298 K. Its molar solubility in a solution buffered at pH 12.0 is:

explanation.en: At pH 12, pOH = 2 and $[\text{OH}^-] = 1.0\times10^{-2}$ M (held constant by the buffer). $s = [\text{Mg}^{2+}] = \dfrac{K_{sp}}{[\text{OH}^-]^2} = \dfrac{1.2\times10^{-11}}{10^{-4}} = 1.2\times10^{-7}$ M. In pure water it would be $(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3} = 1.44\times10^{-4}$ M. $1.2\times10^{-9}$ forgets to square [OH$^-$]; $3.0\times10^{-8}$ wrongly takes $[\text{OH}^-] = 2 \times 10^{-2}$ M.

stem.en: The pH of an aqueous solution of ammonium formate (HCOONH₄) at 298 K is (pK_a of HCOOH = 3.8, pK_b of NH₃ = 4.8):

explanation.en: For a salt of a weak acid and weak base, pH $= 7 + \tfrac12(\text{p}K_a - \text{p}K_b) = 7 + \tfrac12(3.8 - 4.8) = 6.5$. The solution is slightly acidic because formic acid (pK$_a$ 3.8) is a stronger acid than ammonia is a base, so NH$_4^+$ hydrolyses more than HCOO$^-$. 7.5 comes from reversing the subtraction; 7.0 is correct only for ammonium acetate (pK$_a$ ≈ pK$_b$).

stem.en: A solution is saturated with H$_2$S (0.10 M) and contains 0.10 M HCl. For H$_2$S, $K_{a1} = 1.0\times10^{-7}$ and $K_{a2} = 1.3\times10^{-13}$. The concentration of S$^{2-}$ is:

explanation.en: H$_2$S ⇌ 2H$^+$ + S$^{2-}$: $K = K_{a1}K_{a2} = 1.3\times10^{-20}$. With $[\text{H}^+] = 0.10$ M from HCl: $[\text{S}^{2-}] = \dfrac{1.3\times10^{-20} \times 0.10}{(0.10)^2} = 1.3\times10^{-19}$ M. Without added acid, $[\text{S}^{2-}] \approx K_{a2} = 1.3\times10^{-13}$ M. This suppression is why only group-II sulphides (very low K$_{sp}$) precipitate in acidic medium in salt analysis.

stem.en: 1.0 L of a buffer contains 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol CH₃COONa (pK_a = 4.74). Calculate the pH after 0.010 mol of HCl is added (neglect volume change; give two decimal places). (log 0.818 = −0.087)

explanation.en: H$^+$ + CH$_3$COO$^-$ → CH$_3$COOH: acetate $0.10 - 0.01 = 0.09$ mol, acid $0.10 + 0.01 = 0.11$ mol. pH $= 4.74 + \log\dfrac{0.09}{0.11} = 4.74 - 0.087 = 4.65$. The same HCl in 1 L of pure water would give pH 2 — the buffer limits the change to 0.09 units.

stem.en: AgNO₃ is added slowly to a solution that is 0.010 M in both Cl⁻ and CrO₄²⁻. K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and K_sp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Which statement is correct?

explanation.en: AgCl needs $[\text{Ag}^+] = 1.8\times10^{-10}/0.010 = 1.8\times10^{-8}$ M. Ag$_2$CrO$_4$ needs $[\text{Ag}^+] = \sqrt{1.1\times10^{-12}/0.010} = 1.05\times10^{-5}$ M. AgCl reaches saturation at a much lower [Ag$^+$] and precipitates first (the basis of Mohr's method). Comparing K$_{sp}$ values directly is invalid for salts of different stoichiometry.

options.en: Ag₂CrO₄ precipitates first because its K_sp is smaller
AgCl precipitates first; it begins when [Ag⁺] reaches 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ M
Both start precipitating at the same [Ag⁺]
AgCl precipitates first; it begins when [Ag⁺] reaches 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ M
